title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation
audience: Any home-service operator who sets prices or plans monthly revenue, including solo operators.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a home-service business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level the business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. The figure is useful for setting prices, deciding when to hire and checking whether a new channel can pay for itself. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages that go into it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of jobs in a month. They include rent or an office share, insurance, phone and software subscriptions, vehicle registration and loan repayments. Variable costs move with each job. They include consumables, cleaning products used on a job, subcontractor fees and the payment fees charged on each sale. Express variable cost as a percentage of sales: divide the variable cost in a period by the sales in the same period. Bank guidance (ANZ) defines the two cost types and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss. Check that percentage across at least three periods before relying on it, because a single unusual month can mislead.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. The quantity one minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin: the share of each dollar of sales that is left to cover fixed costs. Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 18% becomes 0.18. Then the contribution margin of an 18% variable cost is 0.82.

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source and date. Then compute the contribution margin. Then divide the fixed costs by it. Finally convert the result into a number of jobs at your average job price, and round up to whole jobs, because a part job does not cover costs on its own. The sample plan's fixed cost and variable cost figures are removed here because they are United States figures from 2002. Its break-even figures did not reconcile with its own inputs, so none of them is used. The method is the check: divide fixed costs by the contribution margin, then test the result against inputs you can source.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue and not profit. Then write down the reconciled figure with its inputs and drop the others. A plan that states a break-even figure without its inputs cannot be checked, and a figure that cannot be checked should not be used to set prices.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average job price to get the number of jobs needed each month.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: A two-person residential cleaning business (hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson) has fixed costs of $2,400 AUD a month, variable costs of 18% of sales and an average job price of $180 AUD.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many jobs must the business complete each month to break even, and what should it check before setting prices?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.18, which is 0.82. Break-even revenue is $2,400 AUD divided by 0.82, which is $2,926.83 AUD a month. At $180 AUD a job, that is 16.26 jobs, so the business needs 17 jobs to cover its costs. Each job contributes $147.60 AUD ($180 AUD multiplied by 0.82) towards fixed costs. Before setting prices, check that the 18% includes every job cost, that the $2,400 AUD is a monthly figure, and that $180 AUD is the average price actually charged after discounts.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months

commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from a plan without its inputs
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own inputs and record the source and date of each input before using the result.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs. Do not copy another plan's break-even figure.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $2,400 AUD a month and variable costs are 18% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the client today
Use the price list alone and skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel
